q: CPV-2 is best classified as a:
e: Non-enveloped ssDNA virus, genus Protoparvovirus. The missing envelope is why it is environmentally hardy and resists many disinfectants.

q: Which CPV variant can produce severe panleukopenia-like leukopenia and diarrhoea in cats?
e: CPV-2a, 2b and 2c can infect cats; 2a/2b are usually mild, but CPV-2c can cause severe FPV-like disease. Original CPV-2 did not infect cats.

q: CPV causes its intestinal lesions primarily by destroying:
o: The crypt germinal epithelium, preventing villous renewal
e: Crypt germinal epithelium destruction halts villous renewal, causing villous atrophy, malabsorption and barrier loss with bacterial translocation.

q: The incubation period of CPV is approximately:
e: Incubation is 4 to 14 days; shedding begins around day 4 to 5 (lit review: 4 to 7) and can precede clinical signs.

q: Why is the subclinical form of CPV especially dangerous in a shelter?
o: It is resistant to all disinfectants
Affected animals appear healthy but still shed virus
It cannot be detected by any test
e: Subclinical pups (maternal antibody) or low-titre adults shed virus while looking well, driving silent transmission.

q: The myocardial form of CPV is now rare mainly because:
o: The variant that causes it went extinct
Breeding bitches are vaccinated, protecting neonates
It only ever occurred in cats
e: Myocardial disease follows in-utero or very early infection; maternal vaccination and maternal antibody have made it rare.

q: A 4-month unvaccinated pup has haemorrhagic diarrhoea and a negative faecal ELISA (SNAP). Best next step?
o: Rule out CPV; the test is 100% accurate
Keep in general housing; false negatives are rare
Isolate and pursue qPCR; POCT sensitivity can be ~23 to 34%
Repeat the ELISA on a blood sample
e: POCT specificity is high but sensitivity is low (false negatives common from low viral load or antibody binding). Isolate and confirm with qPCR.

q: Reported performance of the IDEXX SNAP faecal antigen test includes:
e: Specificity ~100% but false negatives up to 51.3%; sensitivity rises to 77 to 80% only at very high faecal viral loads.

q: The reference (gold standard) diagnostic test for CPV is:
e: qPCR has ~94% sensitivity and ~100% specificity. Caveat: recent MLV vaccination can yield a positive result.

q: A healthy dog vaccinated with MLV core on intake tests qPCR-positive on day 10. This most likely reflects:
e: Up to ~23% of recently MLV-vaccinated dogs are qPCR-positive between days 3 and 28, so interpret intake-vaccinated dogs cautiously.

q: Which trend within the first 24 hours of admission has a 100% positive predictive value for survival?
o: A measurable rise in absolute lymphocyte count
e: An early lymphocyte rebound carries a 100% positive predictive value for survival in the cited data.

q: Which is a recognised POOR prognostic indicator in CPV?
e: Poor prognosis: marked persistent leukopenia, severe hypoalbuminaemia, high CK-MB, persistently elevated 72h cortisol, low HCT, hypoglycaemia, hypermagnesaemia.

q: A colleague proposes single-agent cefovecin for all CPV sepsis. The key counter-evidence is:
o: Up to 72% of Gram-negative isolates resisted 3rd/4th-gen cephalosporins and metronidazole
Cefovecin is inactivated by hydrogen peroxide
e: High Gram-negative resistance to 3rd/4th-gen cephalosporins and metronidazole argues for an ampicillin-plus-aminoglycoside backbone once rehydrated.

q: Which antibiotic pairing is favoured for CPV sepsis after rehydration?
e: Ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside gives broad cover; give the aminoglycoside only after rehydration to limit nephrotoxicity.

q: Maropitant should be used cautiously in which group?
e: Maropitant carries a bone-marrow hypoplasia caution in puppies under 8 weeks.

q: Best-supported statement about nutrition in CPV?
o: Withhold all food until vomiting stops 48h
Early enteral nutrition before vomiting resolves improves outcomes
Feeding worsens diarrhoea and should be delayed a week
e: Early enteral feeding (start ~25% RER, build to 100% by day 2 to 4) shortens recovery; NG/NE tubes can stay up to 7 days.

q: Canine parvovirus monoclonal antibody (CPMA, 2024) is best described as:
o: An oral antiviral given for 10 days
A single IV dose raising titres within 24h, with 0% mortality in studies
e: A single IV dose rapidly raises antibody titres and showed 0% mortality with faster clinical resolution in reported studies.

q: Which adjunctive therapy has randomised evidence of NO significant survival benefit?
e: Randomised data show immune plasma gives no significant survival or clinical benefit; hyperimmune plasma lowered 24h shock index and lactate but did not change survival.

q: For hypovolaemic shock in a CPV pup, the crystalloid bolus approach is:
o: 15 to 20 mL/kg over ~15 min, repeated to ~80 to 90 mL/kg total
e: Give 15 to 20 mL/kg boluses over ~15 min, repeated to a total of about 80 to 90 mL/kg, until perfusion is restored.

q: A CPV pup is under 10% dehydrated, BCS 4/9 and responsive. The hybrid model means:
o: Outpatient subcutaneous care only from the start
IV fluids for the first 24h, then step down to SQ/oral care
Inpatient IV care for a full week
e: Hybrid: IV fluids first 24h to correct dehydration, hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia, then SQ and oral care in shelter or foster. Outpatient survival ~80 to 83%.

q: A resource-limited shelter weighs euthanasia. Which finding meets the cited welfare threshold?
e: Cited thresholds for considering euthanasia: BCS under 3/9, recumbency, or non-responsiveness, plus inability to isolate or treat safely.

q: During an outbreak, pups under 5 months in the exposed group should be:
o: Given an MLV DAPP booster and quarantined 14 days
e: Pups under 5 months are high risk regardless of history: booster MLV DAPP and quarantine 14 days, testing any that develop signs.

q: An exposed dog over 5 months with no vaccination history is moderate risk. The key triage tool is:
e: Titre-test moderate-risk dogs; an adequate titre lets you reclassify them as low risk and place them.

q: Regarding foot baths for CPV control:
o: They are the most effective single measure
They are not an effective strategy
e: Foot baths are unreliable (organic-matter accumulation, inadequate contact time) and can spread pathogens. Use dedicated footwear and barrier flooring.

q: Which disinfectant is NOT reliably effective against CPV?
e: Quats are unreliable against non-enveloped CPV. Effective options: accelerated H2O2 (1:32, 10 min), potassium peroxymonosulfate (1%, 10 min), bleach (1:32, 10 min).

q: CPV preferentially targets:
o: Rapidly dividing cells (crypts, lymphoid, marrow, neonatal myocardium)
e: Rapidly dividing populations are most vulnerable, explaining the intestinal, lymphoid, marrow and neonatal myocardial lesions.

q: Disruption of the intestinal mucosal barrier in CPV leads to:
e: Barrier loss allows gut bacteria to translocate, driving endotoxaemia, bacteraemia and potential sepsis.

q: Viral shedding typically begins after infection at about:
e: Shedding starts roughly 4 to 7 days post-infection and can precede clinical signs.

q: The primary route of CPV transmission is:
e: Faecal-oral and oronasal spread predominate, with heavy fomite transmission because the virus is environmentally stable.

q: Under optimal conditions, CPV can persist in the environment for:
e: CPV can remain viable for over a year in cool, shaded, organic-rich conditions, making fomite control critical.

q: The three recognised clinical forms of CPV are:
e: Subclinical, gastroenteric and myocardial; the gastroenteric form is by far the most common.

q: The most common clinical form of CPV is:
e: The gastroenteric form predominates, mainly in pups aged 1 to 6 months.

q: The hallmark haematologic finding of the gastroenteric form is:
e: Severe leukopenia from marrow and lymphoid destruction is the hallmark.

q: Improvement in which sign generally indicates reduced viral shedding?
e: Resolving diarrhoea is generally associated with declining viral shedding.

q: Pale mucous membranes and prolonged CRT in a CPV pup most directly reflect:
o: Anaemia from haemorrhagic diarrhoea or reduced erythrocyte production
e: Anaemia (gut blood loss plus suppressed erythropoiesis) causes pallor and prolonged CRT, though dehydration and sepsis can coexist.

q: The first-line fluid for a CPV patient is:
e: A balanced isotonic crystalloid such as Lactated Ringer's is first line; add dextrose and potassium as indicated.

q: An effective CPV disinfectant and contact time is:
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide 1:32 for 10 min, or bleach 1:32 for 10 min
e: AHP 1:32 (10 min) or bleach 1:32 (10 min) are effective; quats and alcohol are not reliable against non-enveloped CPV.

q: Before applying disinfectant to a contaminated surface you must first:
o: Remove organic matter and clean the surface
e: Organic matter inactivates disinfectants, so physical cleaning must precede disinfection.

q: Heavily contaminated bedding and toys from a CPV case are:
e: Communal washing can spread virus; disposing of heavily contaminated soft items is frequently more practical.

q: Spot cleaning an infected dog's cage is acceptable when:
o: The cage is not visibly soiled
Only on the day of discharge
e: Spot cleaning reduces handling stress and is acceptable if the cage is not visibly soiled; full clean when soiled and after the animal vacates.

q: Outpatient treatment is appropriate for a CPV patient that is:
o: Less than 10% dehydrated, BCS above 3/9, and responsive
e: Outpatient or hybrid care suits stable patients: under 10% dehydrated, BCS above 3/9, responsive.

q: The more reliable test for ongoing viral shedding in a clinically recovered dog is:
e: Animals can shed detectable viral DNA after signs resolve and ELISA turns negative, so qPCR is more reliable for confirming cessation of shedding.

q: If qPCR is unavailable, a clinically recovered CPV dog should be isolated for at least:
e: A minimum 2-week post-recovery isolation is advised when qPCR is unavailable, with bathing before release to reduce fomite spread.

q: Untreated CPV mortality can reach approximately:
e: Untreated mortality can reach around 91%; treated survival is typically 80 to 90%.

q: In non-survivors, serum cortisol at 72 hours post-treatment tends to be:
e: Non-survivors show persistently elevated cortisol at 72 hours, whereas survivors show a decline.

q: Survival in CPV patients receiving appropriate treatment is typically:
e: Treated survival is generally 80 to 90%, with the first 3 to 5 days most critical.

q: CDV is classified as:
e: CDV is an enveloped single-stranded RNA morbillivirus; the envelope makes it labile and easy to inactivate.

q: Vaccines developed in the 1950s to 60s remain effective because CDV has:
e: Only one serotype exists, so cross-protective MLV vaccines remain effective; outbreaks reflect coverage gaps, not antigenic escape.

q: The earliest immunologic effect of CDV infection is:
o: Severe T and B lymphocytopenia with immunosuppression
e: Early infection causes marked T and B lymphocytopenia and immunosuppression that can last weeks.

q: Recently MLV-vaccinated dogs that test RT-PCR positive can be distinguished from field infection because the only undetected vaccine is:
e: MLV CDV replicates in the same cells as wild virus and can be PCR-positive ~2 weeks; the canarypox recombinant is the one not detected.

q: The most common route of CDV transmission is:
o: Direct contact and aerosol between sick and susceptible dogs
e: Direct contact and droplet/aerosol inhalation dominate, so isolating respiratory cases is essential.

q: CDV environmental stability is best described as:
o: Labile, minutes to a few hours when warm
e: As an enveloped virus it is labile; survival is temperature-dependent and short at warm temperatures.

q: Which dogs most help maintain CDV transmission cycles in a shelter?
e: Mildly affected and recovering dogs shed while looking well, sustaining the smouldering cycle.

q: Greater transmission potential on RT-PCR is suggested by:
e: A lower Ct means a higher viral load, indicating greater shedding and transmission potential.

q: An asymptomatic dog vaccinated with MLV 5 days ago tests RT-PCR positive with a very low Ct (high load). Best interpretation?
o: Expected vaccine effect; MLV routinely gives high loads
High load points to wild-type field infection, not vaccine
The dog is immune and can join the adoption ward
Certain false positive; re-run on serum
e: Vaccine virus gives only low load (high Ct); a low Ct (high load) is highly suggestive of active field infection.

q: The CDV clinical course is classically:
e: Biphasic: an early febrile/respiratory phase, then systemic and potentially neurologic disease.

q: The frequently missed earliest sign of CDV is:
e: Early pyrexia (within days to a week) is commonly missed, especially in shelters.

q: CDV neurologic signs:
o: Can appear 1 to 3 weeks or longer after systemic signs resolve
e: Neurologic disease can develop with systemic signs or weeks after they resolve, and carries a poor prognosis.

q: A classic dermatologic sign of CDV is:
e: Digital and nasal hyperkeratosis (hard pad) is described and often linked to neurologic disease.

q: Which examination is recommended in all suspected CDV cases?
e: Ocular signs are common (discharge, KCS, retinal lesions, optic neuritis), so an ocular exam is indicated in all suspects.

q: For CDV there is:
o: No antiviral, so care is supportive and treats secondary infection
e: No antiviral exists; management is supportive with treatment of secondary bacterial infection.

q: When GI signs are present in CDV, the notes recommend:
o: Broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics and B vitamins
e: Broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics are advised for GI signs, with B vitamins.

q: Compared with respiratory and systemic signs, treatment of CDV neurologic disease is:
e: Neurologic disease is often progressive and irreversible, and responds less well than supportive care for other signs.

q: At 56°C (132.8°F), the half-life of CDV is approximately:
e: Half-life is ~4 to 5 minutes at 56°C (132.8°F); survival lengthens at lower temperatures.

q: CDV persists longest at which temperature?
e: At 4°C (39.2°F) the virus can persist 9 to 11 days, so cold conditions make sanitation lapses riskier.

q: Outbreak sanitation for CDV should especially target:
o: Common-contact surfaces such as vehicles, intake pens and staff clothing
e: Because spread is largely contact/fomite over short survival times, target high-traffic shared surfaces.

q: The single most important measure to prevent CDV in shelters is:
o: Vaccinate all dogs at or before intake
e: Intake vaccination is the most important control measure, paired with management that lowers exposure.

q: The preferred shelter CDV vaccine type is:
e: MLV is preferred (lower cost, can occupy binding sites and protect before humoral immunity); rCDV helps against maternal antibody.

q: Given CDV's long incubation, the key alternative to prolonged quarantine of an exposed asymptomatic dog is:
e: Antibody testing can identify protected dogs and shorten or avoid quarantine.

q: An exposed asymptomatic adult has a positive antibody titre and a negative RT-PCR. Correct categorisation?
o: Low risk/protected; clear for adoption or transfer
e: Positive titre plus negative PCR means immune and not shedding: low risk, clear for adoption or transfer.

q: An exposed asymptomatic dog has a negative antibody titre and a negative RT-PCR. This dog is:
o: Susceptible; vaccinate and quarantine away from the outbreak footprint
e: Negative titre plus negative PCR means no current infection but no immunity: susceptible, so vaccinate and quarantine separately.

q: A CDV clean break during an outbreak includes:
o: Mixing new and exposed dogs to build immunity
Vaccinating all incoming dogs at entry, separate housing ~25 ft (7.6 m) away, with separate staff and supplies
Stopping vaccination to avoid PCR confusion
Holding all intake in one shared ward
e: Clean break: vaccinate every incoming dog at entry, house ~25 ft (7.6 m) (ideally a separate ward/building) from exposed dogs, with separate staff and supplies.

q: Why is the puppy CDV booster series extended to 20 weeks of age in shelters?
o: Puppies cannot process antigen until 5 months
High maternal antibody from field-strain-recovered dams can block MLV past 16 weeks
e: Exceptionally high maternal antibody (dams recovered from field strains) blocks MLV beyond the usual 16 weeks, widening the susceptibility window.

q: Which cytologic/histologic finding confirms CDV?
o: Intranuclear basophilic inclusions in hepatocytes only
Both intracytoplasmic and intranuclear eosinophilic inclusion bodies in epithelial cells or astrocytes
Multinucleated giant cells with no inclusions
e: CDV produces both intracytoplasmic and intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions in epithelial cells and astrocytes, a classic board distinction.

q: Regarding a carrier state, CDV:
o: Has no true carrier state but may shed up to 16 weeks
Is shed only by vaccinated dogs
e: There is no true carrier state, though shedding can persist up to 16 weeks and some dogs stay low-level PCR-positive for months with intermittent shedding.

q: A recovered dog that stays low-level RT-PCR positive for months should be:
o: Housed away from susceptibles, ideally with immunised dogs
e: Manage rare persistent low-level positives by keeping them away from susceptibles, ideally in homes with immunised dogs.

q: CIRD is best described as:
o: A multifactorial complex of host, agent and environment
e: CIRD is multifactorial: multiple pathogens plus host and environmental stressors drive disease.

q: The only non-enveloped, environmentally stable CIRD virus is:
e: CAV-2 is the lone non-enveloped (DNA) CIRD virus; it is stable and resists alcohol and quats.

q: CRCoV is nicknamed the lawnmower virus because it:
e: CRCoV denudes respiratory cilia, removing mucociliary clearance and producing classic CIRD signs.

q: For respiratory mucosal protection, the most important element is:
o: Mucosal IgA and intact barriers / innate immunity
e: Intact respiratory barriers, mucociliary function and mucosal IgA matter more than serum IgG/IgM for mucosal pathogens.

q: Mycoplasma cynos virulence is aided by:
e: M. cynos (a wall-less bacterium) uses sialidase to adhere to and damage respiratory epithelium.

q: CIRD pathogens spread mainly by:
o: Aerosolised droplets from coughing and sneezing, plus fomites
e: Spread is largely by respiratory droplets plus fomites (hands, clothing, tools).

q: Coughing and sneezing can propel CIRD pathogens up to about:
e: Droplets travel up to ~6 m (19.7 ft), contaminating open kennels and shared spaces.

q: Which CIRD agents are zoonotic and warrant staff PPE?
e: Both Bordetella and Strep zoo are zoonotic; wear protective clothing, gloves and eye/face protection.

q: Classic uncomplicated CIRD is characterised by:
o: A hacking honking cough with mild nasal discharge, dog usually bright and appetent
e: Typical CIRD is a paroxysmal honking cough with mild discharge; most dogs stay bright, active and appetent.

q: Anorexia and malaise in a CIRD dog most suggest:
e: Anorexia and malaise are red flags for advancing or lower respiratory tract disease.

q: Streptococcus zooepidemicus can progress to:
o: Peracute haemorrhagic pneumonia and sudden death in 24 to 48 hours
e: Strep zoo can cause peracute, haemorrhagic, fibrinosuppurative pneumonia with sudden death over 24 to 48 hours.

q: Which CBC pattern points to descending bacterial pneumonia rather than uncomplicated viral URI?
o: Marked leukocytosis with a left shift (band neutrophils) plus fever
e: An inflammatory leukogram with a left shift plus pyrexia indicates lower-airway bacterial pneumonia; a stress leukogram fits uncomplicated viral URI.

q: For CIRD PCR, the highest-yield dogs to sample are:
o: Asymptomatic dogs in the shelter over 6 weeks
Acutely ill dogs within 1 to 2 days of onset
e: Sample acutely ill dogs within 1 to 2 days; after 5 to 7 days the shedding window closes and PCR loses value (use paired serology).

q: When testing a population during a CIRD outbreak, a reasonable target is:
o: A small representative group of acutely ill dogs (about 5 to 10, or 10 to 30%)
e: Test a small representative group of acutely ill dogs (about 5 to 10, or 10 to 30% of the population), interpreted with clinical context.

q: All CIRD pathogens are inactivated by:
o: Bleach, accelerated hydrogen peroxide and potassium peroxymonosulfate
e: Sodium hypochlorite, accelerated hydrogen peroxide and potassium peroxymonosulfate inactivate all CIRD pathogens.

q: Alcohol sanitiser over 60% works against CIRD agents except:
e: Non-enveloped CAV-2 resists alcohol; enveloped agents are susceptible.

q: Quaternary ammonium is less reliable against CIRD because it:
o: Misses Gram-negative Bordetella and non-enveloped CAV-2 and is inactivated by organic matter
e: Quats have limited Gram-negative and non-enveloped-virus activity and are inactivated by hard water, organic debris and detergent.

q: The essential first step for any disinfectant to work is:
e: Organic debris must be physically removed; disinfectants do not work through organic matter.

q: Cleaning equipment in CIRD wards should:
o: Limit aerosolisation, such as hose-end foamers
e: Limit aerosolisation (hose-end foamers, not pressure sprayers); aerosolisation and humidity spread pathogens.

q: The only CIRD vaccine that induces sterilising immunity is:
e: Only the CDV vaccine gives sterilising immunity; the others reduce infection, shedding and severity but do not prevent colonisation or signs.

q: For respiratory mucosal pathogens, the generally more effective vaccine route is:
o: Intranasal, except CAV-2 where parenteral gives prolonged immunity
e: Intranasal (mucosal) vaccination is generally superior for respiratory agents; CAV-2 is the exception, with parenteral giving 4+ year immunity.

q: The most significant CIRD vaccination error, and its severe systemic risk, is:
o: Injecting a live intranasal Bordetella vaccine SQ; can cause hepatocellular necrosis and liver failure
e: An IN Bordetella vaccine given SQ can cause cellulitis, abscessation and acute hepatocellular necrosis/liver failure; treat with doxycycline.

q: Recommended air changes per hour in shelter housing are about:
e: Aim for 10 to 12 air changes per hour, ideally 100% outdoor air, with separately zoned HVAC for isolation.

q: Healthy dogs with no exposure or signs should be:
o: Vaccinated then released same day without exam
e: Routine quarantine of healthy unexposed dogs is avoided; prolonged LOS is itself the greatest CIRD risk factor.

q: Typical isolation for an uncomplicated, improving CIRD case is:
e: Most improving cases release at 7 to 10 days; decisions weigh resolution of signs, agent shedding and housing risk.

q: Antitussives in CIRD should be:
o: Reserved for severe or debilitating dry cough, with antibiotic cover, and avoided if pneumonia is suspected
e: Reserve antitussives for severe, non-productive cough with antibiotic cover; avoid them with an inflammatory leukogram, fever or consolidation.

q: Long shedders warranting caution before mixing with susceptibles include:
o: CDV, CIV H3N2, Bordetella and Mycoplasma
e: CDV, CIV H3N2, Bordetella and Mycoplasma have prolonged shedding, so use caution before mixing recovered dogs with susceptibles.

q: Streptococcus zooepidemicus requires which antibiotic class, being resistant to doxycycline?
e: Strep zoo needs penicillins/beta-lactams and is resistant to doxycycline.

q: In a Streptococcus zooepidemicus outbreak, the recommended approach is to:
o: Wait for signs in each dog before treating
Prophylactically treat all exposed dogs with a beta-lactam
e: Because disease is rapid and deadly, prophylactically treat all exposed dogs with a beta-lactam (penicillin G or cefovecin).

q: First-line empirical antibiotics for shelter CIRD, under stewardship, should be:
e: Keep first-line to doxycycline or amoxicillin-clavulanate; reserve macrolides and fluoroquinolones for culture-confirmed resistant lower-airway disease.

q: CIV is best classified as:
o: Influenza A (enveloped RNA), subtypes H3N8 and H3N2
e: CIV is an enveloped RNA influenza A virus; the canine subtypes are H3N8 and H3N2.

q: CIV subtypes are defined by:
e: Influenza A is subtyped by its H and N surface glycoproteins (18 H, 11 N identified).

q: H3N2 is notable for:
o: Avian origin and a broader host range including cats, ferrets and guinea pigs
e: H3N2 is avian-origin (Korea 2007, US 2015) with a wider host range than dogs-only H3N8.

q: CIV replicates primarily in:
e: CIV replicates in respiratory epithelium, sloughing cells and exposing tissue to secondary bacteria.

q: CIV spreads by:
o: Aerosols, droplets, direct contact and fomites
e: Spread is respiratory (aerosol/droplet), with direct contact and fomite routes important in shelters.

q: The CIV incubation period is:
e: Incubation is 2 to 5 days; peak shedding at 2 to 4 days can precede signs.

q: Peak CIV shedding occurs:
e: Peak shedding is 2 to 4 days post-infection, so outwardly healthy dogs can be highly contagious early.

q: Regarding a carrier state, CIV:
o: Has none; once shedding stops the dog is not contagious
e: There is no true carrier state; once replication and shedding cease the dog is no longer contagious (H3N2 shedding can be prolonged though).

q: Subclinical shedders make up about what fraction of infected dogs?
e: About 80 to 90% develop signs and 10 to 20% are subclinical shedders, so all exposed dogs are an infectious risk.

q: CIV cannot be reliably distinguished from other CIRD by:
o: Clinical signs alone, so lab testing is needed
e: Signs overlap other CIRD agents; only laboratory testing confirms CIV.

q: Severe CIV disease usually results from:
o: The virus alone in every case
Co-infection or comorbidity, progressing to pneumonia
e: Severe manifestations typically reflect co-infection with other CIRD agents or patient comorbidity.

q: Pneumonia-related CIV fatality is approximately:
e: Mortality is low overall; pneumonia-related fatality is about 5 to 8%, depending on rapid diagnosis and aggressive care.

q: In severe CIV pneumonia, what is the primary mechanism enabling secondary bacterial invasion?
o: Destruction of alveolar macrophages causing hypoxaemia
Necrosis of ciliated columnar epithelium, neutralising the mucociliary escalator
Viral replication in pulmonary capillary endothelium causing DIC
e: CIV destroys ciliated epithelium and the mucociliary escalator, allowing colonisation by Bordetella, Strep zoo and Pasteurella.

q: CIV treatment is mainly:
o: Supportive care while the infection runs its course
e: Care is supportive; antibiotics target secondary bacterial infection or pneumonia.

q: Antibiotics in CIV are warranted:
o: For secondary bacterial infection or pneumonia
e: Reserve antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection or pneumonia, though shelters often treat empirically.

q: Antitussives in CIV are:
o: Of little evidence and contraindicated with a productive cough
e: Antitussives have little evidence in CIV and are contraindicated with a productive cough.

q: For CIV PCR, the correct swab choice and reason is:
o: Cotton-tipped, because virus binds cotton for easier isolation
Synthetic polyester/dacron with plastic shafts, because cotton and wood inhibit PCR
Calcium alginate with wooden shafts, to preserve RNA
Gel-agar swabs, to protect the envelope
e: Cotton fatty acids and wood resins/tannins inhibit PCR and viral assays; use polyester or dacron on plastic/aluminium shafts.

q: A human influenza A patient-side antigen kit is used on a CIV-suspect dog and is negative. This means:
o: The dog is cleared and can leave quarantine
The result is uninformative; a negative cannot clear the dog
e: These kits have poor canine sensitivity: a positive is reliable, but a negative is uninformative and cannot clear an animal from quarantine.

q: Serology (haemagglutination inhibition) for CIV is reliably interpretable:
o: Only after about 10 days of clinical signs
e: Reliable HI detection occurs after ~10 days of signs; a negative before day 10 does not rule out infection. A 4-fold paired-titre rise confirms recent infection.

q: CIV survives on non-porous surfaces for about:
e: As an enveloped virus, CIV survives ~24 to 48 h on non-porous surfaces, 8 to 12 h on porous surfaces, and minutes on hands.

q: Effective CIV disinfectants include:
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide, bleach, quaternary ammonium and potassium peroxymonosulfate
e: Being enveloped, CIV is readily inactivated by AHP, bleach, quats and potassium peroxymonosulfate.

q: Compared with parvovirus, CIV environmental control is:
o: Easier, being a labile enveloped virus
e: CIV is enveloped and labile, so it is far easier to inactivate than the hardy non-enveloped parvovirus.

q: Once a CIV case is suspected, all dogs present should be considered:
o: Exposed or at risk, given high transmissibility
e: High transmissibility and pre-clinical shedding mean all dogs present should be treated as exposed or at risk.

q: Recommended quarantine for exposed dogs is at least:
e: Quarantine exposed dogs a minimum of 14 days, with PCR at days 4 to 7 to release negatives.

q: Subtype-specific isolation for sick dogs is approximately:
o: H3N8 about 7 days, H3N2 about 21 to 28 days
e: H3N8 isolation ~7 to 10 days; H3N2 ~21 to 28 days due to prolonged intermittent shedding.

q: The CIV vaccine is best described as:
o: Non-core, killed, partial protection that does not prevent infection
e: CIV vaccines are killed, non-core, and non-sterilising; two doses 2 to 3 weeks apart with immunity 1 to 2 weeks after the second.

q: Dogs imported from South Korea or China warrant extra precautions because of:
e: High regional H3N2 prevalence justifies aggressive 14-day quarantine and testing for imports from these areas.

q: Why is mass vaccination a flawed strategy to halt an active shelter CIV outbreak?
o: The vaccine is modified-live and causes disease
Killed CIV vaccine needs two doses 2 to 3 weeks apart, with immunity only 1 to 2 weeks after the second
It protects only cats and ferrets
CIV undergoes instant antigenic shift against the vaccine
e: The two-dose killed series with delayed protection cannot stop an outbreak already underway.

q: The overall CIV pattern is:
e: CIV is high-morbidity, low-mortality; most dogs recover with supportive care.

q: A key limitation of CIV recovery immunity is that:
o: CIV mutates quickly, so protection is strain-specific
e: Post-infection antibody persists 5 to 6 years but is strain-specific, and rapid mutation limits cross-protection.

q: The most important feline dermatophyte is:
e: M. canis causes 90%+ of feline dermatophytosis; M. gypseum and Trichophyton are seen more in dogs and rodents.

q: To establish infection, dermatophyte spores require:
e: Spores need microtrauma (humidity maceration, parasites) to breach defences and infect the follicle.

q: Relative to normal feline flora, M. canis:
o: Is NOT part of normal flora, so a positive culture always needs action
e: M. canis is never normal flora; a positive culture means lesions, subtle lesions or mechanical fomite carriage, all requiring action.

q: Recovery from dermatophytosis depends mainly on:
e: Protection is cell-mediated, so antibody titres are clinically useless and immunosuppressed cats may fail to clear infection.

q: Transmission of dermatophytosis occurs by:
o: Direct contact, fomites and sometimes fleas
e: Spread is by contact, contaminated fomites and occasionally fleas; staff can mechanically move spores between cats.

q: Airborne transmission of dermatophytes is:
o: Possible but minimal when husbandry and disinfection are adequate
e: Airborne spread is minor with good sanitation; separate air handling is not required if treatment and cleaning are adequate.

q: Dermatophyte spores persist in the environment for:
e: Spores remain infectious for weeks to months unless the area is thoroughly cleaned.

q: The incubation period for dermatophytosis is:
e: Incubation is 2 to 4 weeks, with follicle infection preceding lesions.

q: Quarantining exposed animals simply to watch for lesions is:
o: NOT recommended; use active diagnostic screening
e: The long incubation makes watch-and-wait quarantine impractical; active screening is preferred.

q: The classic dermatophyte lesion is:
o: Circular alopecia with scaling and inflammation
e: Classic lesions are circular alopecia with scaling and inflammation, though presentation is highly variable.

q: In dogs, lesions that look like classic ringworm are more often:
e: Classic ringworm-looking lesions in dogs are more commonly pyoderma or demodicosis than true dermatophytosis.

q: Juvenile animals (under 1 year) with dermatophytosis tend to have:
e: Young animals more often get severe generalised lesions; adults tend to focal disease.

q: The Wood's lamp examination uses what wavelength, and which pathogen fluoresces apple-green?
e: 365 nm UV; only M. canis fluoresces apple-green among important veterinary pathogens, and only about half of cases do.

q: A negative Wood's lamp examination:
e: A positive is strongly indicative, but a negative never rules out dermatophytosis (Trichophyton and ~50% of M. canis do not fluoresce).

q: On direct microscopy, infected hairs show:
o: Cuffs of refractile ectothrix spores on wider, irregular hairs
e: Infected hairs are wider, irregular and filamentous with ectothrix spore cuffs; 10x confirms hairs, 40x for spores.

q: The gold-standard diagnostic test is:
e: Fungal culture on dermatophyte test medium is the gold standard, typically via the toothbrush technique.

q: The CFU-based P-score is defined as:
o: P1 1-4, P2 5-9, P3 10 or more CFU per plate
e: P-score is colony count: P1 = 1 to 4, P2 = 5 to 9, P3 = 10 or more CFU per plate, overlaid with lesion status.

q: A lesion-free, Wood's-negative cat with a P1 (2 CFU) M. canis culture is best classified and managed as:
o: Fomite (dust-mop) carrier; safeguard re-culture, single lime sulfur dip and adopt
Uninterpretable; quarantine the foster home 6 weeks
e: This is a mechanical fomite carrier: re-culture as a safeguard, do one lime sulfur dip and proceed to adoption (dip-and-go).

q: P3 cats should be:
o: Immediately removed from the general population regardless of lesions
e: P3 (high count, confirmed infection) cats are removed from the general population for strict isolation and full treatment.

q: Over 95% of positive fungal cultures are identified by:
o: Day 10 to 14 (day 10 is a key read point)
e: Most positives appear by day 10 to 14; hold cultures (not animals) for the full 21 days for slower Trichophyton.

q: By day 5, a toothbrush DTM plate from a crusted stray is fully red and covered in heavy, dark, pigmented fuzzy colonies. This is:
o: A true M. canis positive; move to P3 isolation
Saprophytic overgrowth; record HC and reculture
e: Pathogens are pale and turn DTM red as they grow; heavy pigmented overgrowth is saprophytic contamination that masks positives. Record HC and reculture.

q: The shelter systemic treatment of choice is:
o: Itraconazole PO SID for 21 to 28 days
e: Itraconazole 5 to 10 mg/kg PO SID for 21 to 28 days, paired with topical therapy; terbinafine for azole-resistant strains.

q: The first-line topical adjunct is:
e: Lime sulfur twice weekly (8 oz/gallon (236 mL/3.8 L)), applied to the skin base and not rinsed, is first-line topical therapy.

q: The terbinafine dose range for cats is approximately:
e: Terbinafine 10 to 40 mg/kg PO SID (cats toward the higher end), useful for azole-resistant M. canis; monitor ALT.

q: Why is griseofulvin avoided in shelter cats beyond its long cure time and teratogenicity?
o: It causes oral ulcers with lime sulfur
Idiosyncratic, irreversible bone-marrow suppression, lethal in FeLV/FIV-positive cats
e: Griseofulvin can cause idiosyncratic irreversible marrow suppression, accelerated and potentially fatal in retrovirus-positive cats; test FeLV/FIV first.

q: Mycological cure is defined as:
o: Three consecutive weekly negative cultures (two only with lime sulfur plus itraconazole)
e: Three consecutive weekly negative cultures define cure; two suffice only with combined lime sulfur and continuous oral itraconazole.

q: The cornerstone of environmental decontamination is:
o: Mechanical cleaning and removal of spores and hair
Sealing the room for a month
e: Mechanical removal (vacuuming, sweeping, Swiffering) is the single most critical step; disinfect only after thorough cleaning.

q: Which disinfectant set is effective against ringworm spores?
o: Bleach 1:10 or 1:32 (10 min), AHP 1:16, or 2% potassium peroxymonosulfate
e: Effective: bleach (>=10 min), AHP 1:16, 2% potassium peroxymonosulfate, enilconazole 1:100. Quats, chlorhexidine, calcium hypochlorite and 1% KPMS are ineffective.

q: For potassium peroxymonosulfate against ringworm, the effective concentration is:
e: Ringworm needs a 2% solution; 1% is unreliable (unlike parvovirus, where 1% works). Quats fail for both.

q: Cats under treatment are released for adoption when:
o: All co-housed animals reach mycological cure simultaneously
e: Release only when every co-housed animal has reached mycological cure; a negative cat cannot leave if a cage mate is still positive.

q: FPV is best classified as:
e: FPV is a non-enveloped ssDNA parvovirus with a single serotype, closely related to CPV.

q: FPV preferentially infects:
o: Rapidly dividing cells (marrow, lymphoid, intestinal crypts, fetal cerebellum)
e: FPV needs the S-phase of division, so it targets marrow, lymphoid tissue, crypts and fetal/neonatal tissue.

q: FPV enters host cells using the:
e: FPV uses the transferrin receptor to enter and replicate in lymphoid tissue of the oropharynx and gut.

q: Cerebellar hypoplasia in kittens arises from:
o: In-utero or perinatal infection of cerebellar Purkinje cells
e: Perinatal or in-utero Purkinje cell infection produces nonprogressive cerebellar hypoplasia.

q: The leukopenia of FPV results from:
o: Marrow suppression plus neutrophil loss into the gut and lymphoid depletion
e: Marrow suppression, neutrophil losses into the damaged gut, and lymphoid depletion together cause the panleukopenia.

q: The primary transmission route of FPV is:
e: Faecal-oral is primary; transplacental, droplet (with URT co-infection) and fly/flea mechanical spread also occur.

q: FPV environmental survival is approximately:
o: Infective at 4 to 25 C (39.2 to 77°F) for about 13 months
Inactivated by drying within a day
e: FPV is exceptionally hardy, infective at 4 to 25 C (39.2 to 77°F) for around 13 months and persisting over a year in organic matter.

q: Vertical transmission of FPV occurs by:
o: Fetal infection via maternal circulation in mid-gestation
e: The virus crosses the placenta in mid-gestation, infecting the fetus via maternal circulation.

q: The most common clinical form of FPV is:
e: The acute form is most common: biphasic fever, vomiting and fetid/haemorrhagic diarrhoea with severe leukopenia.

q: The peracute form of FPV is characterised by:
o: Sudden death within hours, sometimes mistaken for poisoning
e: Peracute disease kills kittens under 6 months in hours (lethargy to coma to death), often resembling poisoning; near 100% mortality.

q: A leukopenia value indicating a very guarded prognosis is:
e: A WBC under 2000/uL, especially if persistent, carries a very guarded prognosis.

q: Perinatal cerebellar disease in surviving kittens produces:
o: Nonprogressive ataxia and hypermetria with normal mentation
e: Cerebellar hypoplasia gives nonprogressive ataxia, hypermetria and a wide-based stance, with normal mentation.

q: The most serious secondary bacterial invader in FPV is:
e: E. coli is the worst secondary invader once the gut barrier fails, driving bacteraemia and sepsis.

q: The listed alternative antibiotic combination for FPV is:
o: Ampicillin 6.6 mg/kg IM q8h plus gentamicin 4.4 mg/kg q12h
e: Broad-spectrum Gram-negative and anaerobic cover is needed; the listed alternative is ampicillin plus gentamicin.

q: Transfusion in FPV is indicated when:
o: Plasma protein is under 2 g/dL or WBC under 2000/uL
e: Whole blood or plasma at 20 mL/kg/day is indicated when plasma protein is under 2 g/dL or WBC under 2000/uL, monitoring for DIC.

q: Metoclopramide in feline FPV is:
o: Avoided (CTZ receptors are less important in cats and it is contraindicated with GI haemorrhage)
e: Avoid metoclopramide in cats; prefer maropitant or ondansetron. Phenothiazines are also avoided (hypotension in dehydrated cats).

q: Feline recombinant interferon-omega in FPV:
o: Inhibits FPV in culture but leaves clinical signs and survival unchanged
e: It inhibits FPV in cell culture but has not changed signs or survival, so it is not cost-effective for routine shelter use.

q: Which set of agents reliably inactivates FPV?
o: Bleach, potassium peroxymonosulfate, accelerated hydrogen peroxide and calcium hypochlorite
e: Bleach, KPMS, AHP and calcium hypochlorite work; quaternary ammonium and alcohol are ineffective against this hardy non-enveloped virus.

q: Quaternary ammonium against FPV is:
e: Quats (and alcohol) are ineffective against FPV; use bleach, AHP, KPMS or calcium hypochlorite after removing organic matter.

q: Quarantine of apparently healthy, unexposed cats in shelters is:
o: Not recommended, since it increases length of stay
e: Routine quarantine of healthy unexposed cats is avoided; prolonged length of stay is itself a major risk factor.

q: The high-risk exposed category for FPV is:
o: Kittens under 4 months (some say 5) regardless of vaccine status, and unvaccinated cats
Cats over 5 months vaccinated a week prior
Cats with a documented titre over 80
e: Kittens under 4 months and unvaccinated cats are high risk; low risk is over 5 months and vaccinated 5 to 7 days prior.

q: The standard shelter FPV vaccine is:
e: MLV FVRCP given SC is the shelter standard: fast onset and better at overriding maternal antibody than killed vaccine.

q: Successful FPV vaccination produces what kind of immunity?
o: Non-sterilising immunity that only reduces signs
Purely cell-mediated immunity with no antibody
e: Unlike most CIRD agents and CIV, the FPV vaccine produces sterilizing immunity (like CDV), preventing infection of the host.

q: FIV-positive cats requiring FPV protection should receive:
o: Inactivated FPV vaccine, since MLV can cause vaccine-induced panleukopenia
e: FIV-positive cats get inactivated vaccine because MLV can precipitate vaccine-induced panleukopenia; FeLV-positive cats are given inactivated by default but the choice is balanced.

q: For an FPV outbreak, exposed unvaccinated adult cats and the booster choice should be:
o: MLV FVRCP booster (DAPP is the canine vaccine), if not vaccinated within the prior 14 days
e: Cats receive MLV FVRCP, not the canine DAPP; exposed adults are boosted with MLV FVRCP unless vaccinated in the previous 14 days.

q: For FPV antibody titre risk assessment, the correct assay is:
o: A validated feline-specific assay (e.g. Feline VacciCheck); HI titre 80 or higher is protective
e: Canine CPV antibody kits cannot reliably detect FPV antibody in cats; use a feline-specific assay, with an HI titre of 80 or higher considered protective.

q: Passive immunisation for FPV provides protection lasting about:
o: 2 to 4 weeks, with active vaccination delayed 3 to 4 weeks afterward
e: Anti-FPV (or hyperimmune CPV) serum gives 2 to 4 weeks of protection; delay active vaccination 3 to 4 weeks to avoid neutralisation.

q: Kitten mortality with FPV is approximately:
e: Kitten mortality exceeds 90%, peaking at 3 to 5 months as maternal immunity wanes; peracute disease approaches 100%.

q: A haematologic poor-prognosis indicator in FPV is:
e: Hypoalbuminaemia under 30 g/L (with thrombocytopenia and hypokalaemia under 4 mmol/L) signals a poor prognosis and DIC risk.

q: Immunity after recovery from natural FPV infection is:
e: Recovery confers lifelong immunity to reinfection; a single serotype means broad, durable protection.

q: FeLV and FIV are classified as:
o: FeLV oncornavirus and FIV lentivirus, both Retroviridae
e: Both are retroviruses: FeLV is a gammaretrovirus (oncornavirus) and FIV is a lentivirus. Neither is zoonotic.

q: The three outcomes of FeLV infection are:
e: FeLV resolves to abortive (cleared), regressive (provirus latent in marrow) or progressive (systemic, shedding).

q: Abortive FeLV infection shows:
o: Antigen, IFA and PCR all negative
e: A robust immune response clears the virus before dissemination, so antigen, IFA and PCR are all negative; antibody is the only positive marker.

q: Regressive FeLV infection features:
o: Provirus in marrow and organs, IFA negative, possible later reactivation
e: Transient viraemia is suppressed but provirus persists in marrow; IFA is negative, PCR variable/low-copy, with low disease risk unless reactivated.

q: Progressive FeLV infection features:
o: Spread to multiple organs with shedding; antigen, IFA and PCR generally positive
e: The immune response fails; viraemia spreads, the cat sheds and is continuously infectious, and antigen, IFA and PCR are generally positive.

q: The primary FeLV transmission route is:
e: FeLV is the 'friendly-cat' virus, spread by social oronasal contact and efficient maternal/nursing transmission.

q: The primary FIV transmission route is:
e: FIV is the 'fighting-cat' virus, spread by deep bite wounds inoculating saliva into tissue.

q: FIV-positive and FIV-negative cats can cohabit if:
e: Because FIV needs bite-wound inoculation, compatible non-aggressive cats can cohabit with little risk.

q: The zoonotic potential of FeLV and FIV is:
e: Neither feline retrovirus is zoonotic.

q: FIV infectivity in milk is counteracted by:
o: Concurrent FIV antibody that protects nursing neonates
e: FIV antibody shed concurrently in milk neutralises the virus and protects most nursing neonates, unlike FeLV where nursing is a major route.

q: Pathognomonic signs of feline retroviral infection are:
o: None; many cats are asymptomatic for long periods
e: There are no pathognomonic signs; disease comes from chronic effects (anaemia, neoplasia, inflammation, opportunistic infection).

q: In neonatal cats, FeLV can cause:
e: FeLV can cause fading kitten syndrome; most signs otherwise reflect chronic retroviral disease.

q: A 2-year-old cat with dyspnoea and a cranial mediastinal mass with pleural effusion most suggests:
o: Progressive FeLV driving mediastinal/thymic T-cell lymphoma
Regressive FIV with a mast cell tumour
e: FeLV classically causes mediastinal/thymic T-cell lymphoma in young cats; FIV is linked to B-cell lymphoma (GI/nasal) in older cats.

q: Point-of-care screening detects:
o: Soluble FeLV p27 antigen and FIV antibody
e: POC tests detect FeLV p27 antigen and FIV antibody; whole blood is more sensitive than serum/plasma for p27.

q: The most sensitive sample for FeLV p27 detection is:
e: Whole blood is more sensitive than serum or plasma for p27 antigen detection.

q: IFA for FeLV is:
o: Negative in regressive and positive in progressive infection
e: IFA detects p27 in leukocyte/platelet cytoplasm: negative in regressive infection, positive in progressive (marrow-infected) disease.

q: A low proviral copy number on quantitative FeLV PCR indicates:
e: Low copy number marks regressive infection (prolonged survival); high copy number marks progressive infection with higher morbidity/mortality.

q: A kitten with a positive FIV antibody test should be:
o: Retested until 5 to 6 months, when maternal antibody is gone
e: Under 6 months a positive is almost always maternal antibody (vertical FIV is rare); retest until 5 to 6 months before calling it infected.

q: After a known recent exposure, the recommended retest windows are:
o: 30 days for FeLV and 60 days for FIV
e: FeLV p27 antigenaemia can take up to 30 days and FIV antibody up to 60 days; testing too early gives false negatives.

q: An unweaned kitten tests whole-blood FeLV-antigen positive at intake. The best action is:
o: Euthanise immediately to protect the population
Isolate from unrelated litters and retest at adoption age
Declare abortive infection and clear it
e: Many FeLV-antigen-positive neonates revert by adoption age as early transient antigenaemia transitions to regressive infection (typically within ~16 weeks); never euthanise a healthy unweaned kitten on a single intake positive.

q: In the environment, FeLV and FIV are:
o: Short-lived, not airborne, not spread by casual handling
e: Both are fragile retroviruses; no special sanitation is needed, and they are not airborne or spread by casual contact.

q: A key iatrogenic transmission route to prevent for FeLV/FIV is:
o: Blood transfusion and contaminated invasive instruments
e: Both transmit efficiently via transfusion and cross-contaminated invasive instruments.

q: Pooling samples or testing one cat as a proxy for a group is:
o: Not appropriate; it reduces test sensitivity
e: Pooling lowers sensitivity and proxy testing is invalid; test cats individually.

q: Before entering group housing, cats must be:
e: A negative FeLV result is required before group housing; FIV testing may be optional if cats are compatible and stress is low.

q: The FeLV vaccine is best described as:
o: Non-core, for at-risk cats, given after determining status, from 8 weeks, 2 doses 3 to 4 weeks apart
e: FeLV vaccine is non-core for at-risk cats; determine status first (no value vaccinating infected cats), from 8 weeks, 2 doses 3 to 4 weeks apart.

q: The FeLV vaccine is given low on the left hind limb because:
o: A later injection-site sarcoma can be removed with clean margins by hindlimb amputation
e: Distal-limb placement means an adjuvant-associated feline injection-site sarcoma can be excised with clean margins via amputation.

q: FIV vaccination in shelters is:
e: FIV vaccine is non-core and not recommended in shelters: it covers only subtypes A and D and induces antibody indistinguishable from infection on common POC tests.

q: Outbreaks of FeLV or FIV in a shelter are:
o: Not expected, given chronic infection and low transmission
e: Both are chronic, low-transmission infections, so epidemic outbreaks are not expected; management focuses on testing and segregation.

q: The effect of FeLV versus FIV on lifespan is:
o: FeLV shortens lifespan; FIV is variable and often normal
Both always fatal within a year
FIV shortens lifespan; FeLV is normal
e: FeLV typically shortens lifespan (many die within ~5 years); FIV is variable and frequently normal.

q: Why is routine FeLV/FIV testing not recommended for TNR community cats?
o: Community seroprevalence mirrors owned cats, screening wastes resources, and sterilisation itself curbs transmission behaviours
Testing always gives false positives outdoors
e: Positives do not add to the threat if cats remain outdoors; resources are better spent on sterilisation, which removes nursing (FeLV) and fight-bite (both) transmission.

q: FIP is caused by:
e: FIP is a complication of feline coronavirus, a large enveloped RNA alphacoronavirus prone to mutation.

q: The prevailing explanation for how FIPV arises is:
o: Horizontal transmission of FIPV between cats
Internal mutation of FECV to FIPV within an individual cat
e: The internal mutation theory: FECV mutates to macrophage-tropic FIPV within an individual cat, commonly involving the S gene and 3c/7a/7b.

q: The most commonly implicated mutation site for the FECV-to-FIPV switch is:
e: The spike (S) protein gene (with accessory genes 3c, 7a, 7b) is most commonly implicated; S protein governs cell entry.

q: Primarily effusive (wet) FIP results from:
o: Strong humoral with weak or absent cellular immunity, via Type III hypersensitivity
e: Strong humoral plus weak cellular immunity produces immune-complex vasculitis (Type III hypersensitivity) and effusion; a strong cell-mediated response can prevent disease.

q: The proportion of FCoV-seropositive cats that develop FIP is:
e: FIP is uncommon: under 3% of seropositive cats and fewer than 5% of shedders develop it.

q: FECV is transmitted mainly by:
o: The oro-nasal/faecal-oral route, especially shared litter boxes
e: FECV spreads oro-nasally via infected faeces, with shared litter boxes a key route in multi-cat settings.

q: Compared with adults, kittens 8 to 16 weeks shed FECV at levels about:
e: Primary shedding in kittens 8 to 16 weeks averages ~10,000 times that of adults, so mixing unrelated litters is discouraged.

q: FIPV itself is:
o: Readily transmitted cat to cat faecal-orally
Not transmitted faecal-orally (it cannot replicate in epithelial cells); horizontal spread is extremely rare
e: FIPV has lost epithelial tropism, so it is not spread faecal-orally and is essentially non-contagious between cats.

q: A shelter FIP cluster usually reflects:
o: A novel mutant virus spreading between cats
Husbandry and housing creating high FCoV loads and amplified risk factors
e: Clusters reflect conditions that amplify FCoV exposure and host risk, not a contagious mutant virus.

q: A young cat has a classic FIP effusion (A:G 0.42) and a standard FCoV RT-PCR on the fluid is positive. The best interpretation is:
o: Definitive for FIP, since FECV never leaves the gut
It confirms FCoV but does not prove mutation to FIPV, because FECV circulates in monocytes and reaches effusions
A guaranteed false positive from maternal antibody
Invalid, since RT-PCR detects only Type II
e: Because enteric FECV circulates in monocytes and reaches extra-intestinal sites, a positive standard FCoV PCR confirms exposure, not mutated FIPV.

q: The RT-PCR plus S-gene-mutation assay has high specificity but low sensitivity mainly because:
o: The mutation is an individual, variable event (3c/7a/7b escape the primers) and it misses Type II FCoV
e: FIP mutations are individual and variable, so novel point mutations escape the S-gene primers, and the assay does not capture Type II FCoV.

q: The definitive antemortem diagnostic test for FIP is:
o: Immunohistochemistry showing FCoV antigen within macrophages in pyogranulomatous lesions
e: Demonstrating viral antigen inside macrophages within classic lesions (IHC or direct immunofluorescence) is the gold standard, ruling out bystander enteric FCoV.

q: The two clinical forms of FIP are:
e: FIP presents as effusive (wet) or non-effusive (dry), often with mixed features; the form reflects the immune response.

q: Neurologic signs in FIP occur primarily with the:
e: Neurological disease is mainly a non-effusive manifestation; ocular lesions occur in both forms.

q: A classic FIP effusion is:
o: Straw-yellow, viscous, high-protein, frothing when shaken, low cellularity
e: A modified-transudate/non-septic exudate: straw-yellow, viscous, protein over 3.5 g/dL, low cellularity, frothing on shaking.

q: On FIP effusion analysis, which statement about the A:G ratio is correct?
o: A:G under 0.5 has ~89% positive predictive value; A:G over 1 has ~91% negative predictive value
A:G is not useful in effusions
e: An effusion A:G under 0.5 has ~89% PPV for FIP; an A:G over 1 has ~91% NPV against it.

q: The Rivalta test for FIP effusions is best described as:
o: High sensitivity (91-98%) but low specificity (66-80%), so a negative is reassuring but false positives occur with sepsis/neoplasia
e: Rivalta is sensitive but not specific; a negative reliably lowers suspicion, while positives also occur in septic or neoplastic effusions.

q: Ocular signs in FIP include:
o: Uveitis, iritis, retinitis and keratic precipitates
e: Uveitis, iritis, retinitis and keratic precipitates occur, and ocular lesions are seen in both effusive and non-effusive forms.

q: Once clinical signs appear, untreated FIP mortality is:
e: Untreated FIP is nearly always fatal once signs appear, often within days to weeks.

q: The two antiviral agents central to modern FIP therapy are:
e: GS-441524 is a nucleoside analog and GC376 is a 3C-like protease inhibitor (your notes' 'GS-376' is a typo for GC376); remdesivir is the GS-441524 prodrug.

q: Historical prednisolone and cyclophosphamide therapy for FIP:
o: Slows progression without altering the ultimate outcome
e: These palliative drugs may slow progression but do not change the fatal outcome; modern antivirals do.

q: Per the most current status, FIP treatment in the US is:
o: No FDA-approved drug exists, but compounded oral GS-441524 is legally obtainable under FDA enforcement discretion since June 2024
e: There is still no FDA-approved FIP drug, but since 1 June 2024 the FDA exercises enforcement discretion allowing veterinary-prescribed compounded GS-441524. Confirm current status.

q: FCoV survives in a dry environment for up to:
e: FCoV survives up to ~7 weeks dry, which underpins the conservative 2-month wait before introducing a new cat to a home where an FIP cat lived.

q: Because FCoV is an enveloped virus, shelter sanitation:
o: Uses standard detergents/disinfectants that inactivate it immediately, so rooms are cleaned and reused promptly
e: Enveloped FCoV is readily inactivated by standard shelter disinfectants; unlike the home 2-month rule, shelters clean, disinfect and reuse the space promptly.

q: The most important sanitation focus for limiting FCoV load is:
o: Litter-box management (frequent scooping and cleaning of scoops) and not mixing litters
e: Faecal-oral FECV load is controlled by litter-box hygiene, one litter per enclosure, and avoiding mixing of unrelated litters.

q: A shelter FIP outbreak (genetically unrelated cats) is defined as incidence greater than:
e: In an unrelated shelter population, over 1% is an outbreak; a cattery threshold is over 10%, hoarding 5 to 10%.

q: In a breeding cattery, an FIP outbreak is defined as incidence greater than:
e: Related, densely housed cattery cats tolerate a higher baseline, so the outbreak threshold is over 10%.

q: FIP vaccination in shelters is:
o: Not useful; the one intranasal product shows minimal efficacy
e: The available intranasal FIP vaccine shows minimal efficacy and is not a useful shelter control measure; titres are also unhelpful.

q: The cornerstone of FIP outbreak management is:
o: Mass antiviral treatment of every cat
Risk assessment, reducing environmental pathogen load, and a clean break
Mass fecal RT-PCR with euthanasia of shedders
e: Management is risk assessment, lowering environmental FCoV, and a clean break between affected and new populations; mass PCR is not useful.

q: Greatest FIP risk is in cats aged:
o: Up to 3 years, especially 4 to 16 months
e: Risk concentrates under 3 years, especially 4 to 16 months; in Australia 80% of cases were under 2 years.

q: FHV-1 establishes latency primarily in the:
o: Trigeminal ganglia and cool URT sites
e: FHV-1 becomes latent in the trigeminal ganglia and cool URT tissues, reactivating with stress.

q: FCV is best described as:
o: A non-enveloped RNA virus with many strains in one serotype
e: FCV is a non-enveloped, rapidly mutating ssRNA virus; one serotype but many antigenically distinct strains.

q: After infection, the proportion of cats that become latent FHV-1 carriers is at least:
e: At least 80% of infected cats become lifelong latent carriers, underlying the 50 to 97% seroprevalence.

q: Bordetella bronchiseptica predisposes to co-infection mainly by:
e: Bordetella destroys respiratory cilia, removing a key mucosal defence and predisposing to secondary infection.

q: A pathophysiologic reason perfect biosecurity cannot eliminate shelter URTD is:
o: The virus is airborne over long distances
e: Stress-induced recrudescence of latent FHV-1 means new cases arise even with flawless biosecurity.

q: The most common route of URTD spread in shelters is:
e: Fomite transmission dominates (other than FHV-1 recrudescence); true aerosol is unlikely.

q: Sneezed respiratory droplets travel approximately:
e: Droplets travel ~1 to 1.3 m (3.3 to 4.3 ft), so facing cage banks should be at least 1.3 m (4.3 ft) apart.

q: Regarding ventilation, feline URTD is:
o: Not airborne, so separate per-cage ventilation is not necessary
e: URTD is not airborne; good air quality matters but separate per-cage ventilation is not required.

q: FHV-1 survives in a damp environment for up to about:
e: FHV-1 is fragile, surviving ~18 h in damp conditions and less when dry; it is easily disinfected.

q: FCV survives at room temperature for at least:
e: FCV is hardy, surviving at least 28 days at room temperature, which drives its fomite spread.

q: Oral and tongue ulcers are most characteristic of:
e: Tongue and oral ulcers are classic for FCV; FHV-1 favours corneal/dendritic ulcers.

q: Dendritic corneal ulcers point to:
e: Dendritic corneal ulceration is characteristic of FHV-1 keratitis.

q: Chemosis with conjunctivitis progressing from unilateral serous to bilateral mucopurulent suggests:
e: Chemosis with that progression is characteristic of Chlamydia felis.

q: Febrile limping syndrome is uniquely associated with:
e: Self-limiting febrile lameness after infection or vaccination is unique to FCV.

q: Virulent systemic FCV is presumptively diagnosed by the triad of:
o: Mild sneezing, normal temperature, single case
High mortality, severe vasculitis/cutaneous oedema (head/paws), and rapid in-enclosure transmissibility
Cerebellar ataxia, low WBC, and chronic course
e: VS-FCV needs high mortality, severe vasculitis with head/paw oedema, and rapid spread; routine FCV vaccine does not protect.

q: The antiviral and dose used for FHV-1 is:
e: High-dose famciclovir (90 mg/kg PO q8h) outperforms low dose for FHV-1; topical idoxuridine/cidofovir treat keratitis.

q: The first-choice antibiotic for M. felis, Bordetella and C. felis is:
o: Doxycycline 5 mg/kg q12h or 10 mg/kg q24h
e: Doxycycline is first-line empiric therapy for acute bacterial feline URTD; give liquid with a water/food flush.

q: Penicillins and cephalosporins are ineffective against Mycoplasma because:
o: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so beta-lactams that target peptidoglycan cannot work
They are inactivated by feline saliva
e: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, so peptidoglycan-targeting beta-lactams fail; use doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone.

q: Amoxicillin is an acceptable first-line URTD choice only when:
o: Mycoplasma or Chlamydia are not suspected
e: Amoxicillin (or amoxicillin-clavulanate) is acceptable only when Mycoplasma and Chlamydia are not suspected.

q: To prevent oesophageal stricture, doxycycline should be:
o: Given as a liquid followed by water or food
Given on an empty stomach with no follow-up
e: Doxycycline hyclate tablets can cause feline oesophageal strictures; use the liquid and follow with water or food.

q: Lack of response to URTD treatment within 5 to 7 days indicates:
o: The need for further diagnostic workup
e: No response in 5 to 7 days suggests additional medical or drug-related problems needing further workup.

q: Effective disinfectants against FCV are:
o: 1:32 bleach, potassium peroxymonosulfate or accelerated hydrogen peroxide
e: Non-enveloped FCV resists quats and alcohol; use 1:32 bleach, KPMS or AHP.

q: Alcohol-based hand sanitiser in feline URTD is:
o: Ineffective against FPV and of limited efficacy against FCV (non-enveloped capsids resist alcohol)
e: Alcohol cannot disrupt non-enveloped capsids; soap-and-water washing or AHP wipes are mandatory for FCV/FPV.

q: A cat given an intranasal MLV FVRCP vaccine 5 days ago has a positive FHV-1 and Mycoplasma PCR. The best interpretation is:
o: Definitive active FHV-1 field infection requiring antivirals
The FHV-1 positive may be recent IN vaccine shedding (false-positive for 1 to 3 weeks), and Mycoplasma is often normal flora, so PCR does not prove causation
Mycoplasma is the sole primary pathogen, start amoxicillin for 4 weeks
The swab type invalidated the test
e: IN MLV vaccination causes false-positive FHV-1/FCV PCR for 1 to 3 weeks, and a Mycoplasma-positive does not prove primary disease.

q: The single greatest risk factor for URTD in shelter cats is:
e: Length of stay is the single greatest risk factor; URTD risk rises over the first 2 weeks then stabilises around 3 weeks.

q: A staff workflow that lowers clinical URTD rates is:
e: Dedicating/separating staff by section reduces fomite spread and was associated with significantly lower URTD rates.

q: Group housing of cats should use groups of:
e: Keep groups small (5 or fewer) and stable; regrouping is associated with FHV-1 reactivation.

q: The ideal management of kittens too young for adoption is:
o: Foster care, bypassing the shelter environment
e: Kittens too young to adopt should go directly to foster, avoiding the high-shedding shelter environment.

q: Routine vaccination of shelter cats against Bordetella and Chlamydia is:
e: Routine Bordetella and Chlamydia vaccination is not recommended for shelter cats; core MLV FVRCP is given at intake.

q: Why is routine 14-day quarantine of healthy incoming cats generally advised against?
o: It is too cheap to bother with
It increases length of stay, the single greatest URTD risk factor; prioritise intake vaccination, good housing and low LOS instead
e: Routine quarantine raises LOS (the top risk factor); better to vaccinate at intake, house well and minimise LOS.

q: Streptococcus canis and S. zooepidemicus in cats are best distinguished by:
o: They are the same organism under two names

S. canis causes outbreak necrotising sinusitis, meningitis, or necrotising fasciitis/toxic shock (up to 30% fatality); S. zooepidemicus is isolated with or without respiratory signs and needs a special PCR request
S. canis is always subclinical; S. zooepidemicus is always fatal
e: They are distinct Gram-positive species with different clinical pictures; S. zooepidemicus is excluded from routine feline PCR panels and both are zoonotic.

q: A cat on a dairy farm develops depressed mentation, ataxia, blindness, and oculonasal discharge after exposure to raw milk from sick cows. What should be considered?
o: Routine FHV-1 recrudescence; no special testing needed
H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza; this history and neurologic presentation is consistent with the 2024–2025 US dairy-associated outbreak
Chlamydia felis; treat with 4 weeks of doxycycline
This is not a reportable concern
e: Severe neurologic signs plus farm/raw milk exposure should raise suspicion for H5N1, which has caused severe, often fatal disease in farm cats during the 2024–2025 US outbreak.

q: Doxycycline is being considered for a 3-week-old kitten with M. felis-associated URTD. The correct approach is:
o: Avoid it entirely until 4 weeks of age
It can be used safely under 4 weeks; enamel discoloration from tetracyclines is a cosmetic issue only in cats, not a functional health concern
Use a double dose to compensate for reduced absorption
e: Doxycycline is labelled for cats over 4 weeks but can be used safely below that age too, since the enamel-staining effect of tetracyclines is cosmetic only in cats.

q: The labelled dose of transdermal mirtazapine (Mirataz) for feline appetite stimulation is:
o: 2 mg/kg once daily, adjusted to body weight
A fixed 2 mg/cat once daily (a 1.5-inch ribbon to the inner pinna), regardless of body weight
e: Mirataz is dosed as a fixed 2 mg/cat, not weight-based — unusual among feline drugs. Oral mirtazapine is dosed per-cat too: 1.88 mg/cat q24h or 3.75 mg/cat q72h.

q: Which age group is most susceptible to Chlamydia felis infection?
o: Kittens around 5 to 12 weeks of age, with susceptibility falling as cats mature
Adult cats 1 to 5 years, equally across kittens and adults
e: Chlamydia felis disease is seen most commonly in kittens around 5 to 12 weeks old; susceptibility decreases with age. Adequate individual housing with routine biosecurity and hygiene should be sufficient to manage spread.

q: Daily spot cleaning of a cat's own housing unit is:
o: Never acceptable; full disinfection is always required
Acceptable for routine URI and healthy cats, but insufficient once FCV is suspected, which needs more vigorous cleaning/disinfection (1:32 bleach, 1% potassium peroxymonosulfate, or AHP)
Only acceptable for FHV-1, never for any bacterial agent
Equivalent to full-cage disinfection for every pathogen
e: Spot cleaning reduces stress and is fine for routine cases; suspected FCV contamination needs the more resistant-virus-appropriate disinfectant protocol.

q: Which diagnostic test is the gold standard for detecting Mycoplasma haemofelis infection?
o: Direct blood smear showing organisms on RBC surfaces
PCR for hemoplasma (blood); most sensitive and specific; can speciate
e: PCR is the gold standard. Blood smear sensitivity is LOW — parasitemia is cyclic and organisms are absent on the smear during non-parasitemic phases. Howell-Jolly bodies and stain artifacts can also mimic hemoplasma on smear.

q: A 3-year-old FIV-positive cat presents with severe lethargy, pale mucous membranes, PCV of 12%, and PCR-confirmed Mycoplasma haemofelis. Which treatment approach is correct?
o: Prednisone alone; antibiotics are ineffective against Mycoplasma
Doxycycline 10 mg/kg PO once daily × 28 days; add prednisolone if immune-mediated hemolysis is suspected; consider blood transfusion if PCV <15%
Ronidazole 30 mg/kg once daily for 14 days, as for Tritrichomonas
e: Doxycycline (once daily in cats to reduce esophageal stricture risk from twice-daily) is first-line. Prednisolone is added if an immune-mediated component is present. Blood transfusion is indicated for severe anemia (PCV <15%). Ronidazole is for Tritrichomonas foetus, not hemoplasma.

q: Which statement about Mycoplasma haemofelis and flea control in shelters is correct?
o: Fleas are not a significant route of hemoplasma transmission — bite wounds are the primary route
Fleas (Ctenocephalides felis) are the primary transmission vector; strict flea control is the most important prevention measure in a shelter
Hemoplasma is transmitted by ticks, not fleas
Hemoplasma vaccination is available and provides complete protection
e: Ctenocephalides felis (cat flea) is the primary vector for M. haemofelis. Flea-free shelter status substantially reduces hemoplasma transmission. Blood donor cats must also be PCR-screened before use.

q: An unvaccinated 8-week-old puppy presents with acute, hemorrhagic diarrhea, vomiting, lethargy, and a CBC showing leukopenia. What is the highest-priority first action?
o: Run a Giardia ELISA and treat empirically with fenbendazole
Immediately isolate the puppy and run a CPV fecal antigen ELISA — treat as CPV until proven otherwise
Move the puppy to the general population pending culture results
Administer oral metronidazole and observe for 48 hours before testing
e: An unvaccinated puppy with hemorrhagic diarrhea, vomiting, leukopenia, and lethargy is CPV until proven otherwise. Immediate isolation and CPV fecal antigen test are the first steps — delay in isolation allows exposure of susceptible animals in the population.

q: A recently vaccinated dog tests positive on the IDEXX SNAP CPV fecal antigen test 3 days after receiving an MLV DAPP vaccine. How should this result be interpreted?
o: This confirms active CPV infection; begin intensive treatment immediately
This is likely a vaccine-induced false positive; MLV CPV vaccine virus is shed in feces for up to 2 weeks post-vaccination; clinical signs and CBC (leukopenia) are needed to distinguish from true CPV
The test is unreliable and should be discarded
Transfer to an emergency hospital immediately
e: MLV CPV vaccine virus is shed in feces for up to 5 days and occasionally up to 2 weeks after vaccination, causing false-positive antigen tests. Clinical signs (severity of GI illness, leukopenia on CBC) and PCR confirmation are needed when the result is ambiguous.

q: During a shelter diarrhea cluster affecting 5 dogs in the same intake ward, which disinfectant is appropriate for both Salmonella and CPV contamination?
o: Quaternary ammonium compounds (quats) at standard dilution
Accelerated hydrogen peroxide (AHP) 1:32 with 10 min contact time
e: AHP 1:32 with ≥10 min contact is effective against both CPV (non-enveloped) and Salmonella. Quats FAIL against CPV. Bleach at 1:100 is too dilute for CPV (1:32 required). Alcohol does not reliably kill non-enveloped viruses like CPV.

q: Which pathogen causing feline diarrhea requires 6% hydrogen peroxide or steam cleaning because standard bleach dilutions are ineffective?
e: Cryptosporidium oocysts are highly resistant to chlorine disinfectants including standard bleach dilutions. Steam (≥60°C (140°F)) or 6% hydrogen peroxide (30 min contact) are required. This is the most challenging pathogen to decontaminate in a shelter.

q: A long-term cat ward sees an abrupt URI spike during a winter intake surge. Sanitation is unchanged and no new pathogen entered, but major construction (daily drilling, vibrations) just began next door. The primary driver is:
o: Increased agent virulence from structural shifting of the building
Environmental stressors (loud, unfamiliar noise; unpredictable events) triggering host immunosuppression and recrudescence of latent carriers such as FHV-1
Mechanical vectors (fleas, mosquitoes) failing to circulate fresh air
Mutation of Mycoplasma into cell-wall-producing bacteria from vibration
e: Stress is a host factor in the epidemiological triad. Noise and unpredictability immunosuppress the resident population, recrudescing latent FHV-1 — an 'outbreak' with no new pathogen and identical sanitation.

q: Thirty cats from a hoarding case arrive; 80% have severe painful chronic stomatitis and suspected FCV carriage. Before committing to long-term on-site mass treatment, the most critical questions are:
o: Which chew toys are safe, and can nail trims precede antibiotic choice?
How hard is the agent to kill with alcohol, and will the cats need intensive grooming?
Welfare during prolonged treatment, prognosis for recovery, and whether resources and funds allow treatment without compromising basic care for the general population
Can the whole cohort go straight to general adoption to cut length of stay?
e: Capacity for Care is dynamic: if treating the infected cohort drops baseline care of the general population below minimum standards, C4C is exceeded. Welfare, prognosis and resource impact are the decisive questions.

q: An intake room is contaminated with feline calicivirus (non-enveloped) and feline panleukopenia virus. A technician proposes a quaternary ammonium compound because it is cheap and pleasant-smelling. You should:
o: Approve — quats reliably disrupt the capsids of non-enveloped shelter pathogens
Deny — non-enveloped viruses resist quats; use an oxidizing disinfectant (accelerated hydrogen peroxide or 1:32 bleach)
Switch to an alcohol hand-rub wipe-down, which sterilizes against parvovirus
Skip chemical disinfection and rely on daily brushing/grooming
e: Non-enveloped viruses (FCV, FPV/parvo) lack a lipid envelope and resist quats and alcohol. Effective decontamination requires an oxidizing agent — AHP or 1:32 bleach.

q: An FPV epidemic curve shows a massive sharp peak on Day 1 with gradual decline, then from Day 8 a series of successively higher peaks ~3–4 days apart. Interpretation:
o: Continuous common source that has mutated into an airborne pathogen
Began as a point source (e.g., one infectious litter admitted together) and, from an isolation/sanitation failure, transitioned to a propagated, animal-to-animal outbreak
Data error — FPV never causes multiple peaks because of maternal antibody
Steady-state fluctuations proving the quat disinfectant neutralized the virus
e: A point-source spike followed by successive incubation-spaced peaks signals transition to a propagated outbreak — isolation or sanitation has broken down.

q: During a CDV outbreak, an asymptomatic 6-month-old dog housed with a shedding puppy has a strongly positive point-of-care CDV antibody titer. Best management:
o: 14-day quarantine, because positive titers over 5 months are usually false positives
Because he is over 5 months and clinically normal, the positive titer correlates strongly with protection — categorize low risk and move toward adoption without mandatory quarantine
Invalid test — redraw blood only 14 days after exposure ends so maternal antibody wanes
e: In asymptomatic animals over 5 months, a positive CDV/CPV/FPV titer correlates with near-sterilizing protection. Maternal-antibody skew is the concern only in animals under 5 months.

q: During concurrent S. zooepidemicus and FCV outbreaks, the supervisor orders accelerated hydrogen peroxide mixed at triple label concentration. Why intervene?
o: Tripling concentration converts non-enveloped calicivirus into a point-source pathogen
Chemical agents lose all efficacy against Gram-positives at higher concentration
Stronger-than-label disinfectant is not more effective and causes harm — caustic residues irritate the respiratory tract and mucosa, increasing host susceptibility
Changing concentration is only permitted for vector-borne mange
e: Over-concentrating disinfectant adds no benefit and leaves caustic residues that damage respiratory and ocular mucosa and paw pads, raising susceptibility and mimicking a URTD/CIRD outbreak.

q: A county shelter legally obligated to accept strays has a VS-FCV outbreak (50% mortality), exceeded isolation capacity, and maxed staff hours. The director demands total depopulation of all cats. Per ASV standards:
o: Approve immediate building-wide depopulation as the standard response to high-morbidity outbreaks

Deny depopulation as the initial response — implement cohort risk stratification, create a clean break, use titers where appropriate, and consult municipal/legal counsel to temporarily restrict or divert intake while arranging offsite options
Stop all data collection and run PCR panels on healthy dogs
Open communal rooms to the public to speed adoptions and reduce crowding
e: Depopulation is a last resort. The alternative is cohort stratification (affected/exposed/unexposed), a clean break, titer triage, and — given a legal intake mandate — working with administrators and counsel to restrict or divert intake.

q: A vet uses an FDA-approved human antibiotic extra-label for deep pyoderma in 45 confiscated dogs (no veterinary alternative). Which statement on records/labeling is accurate?
o: Shelter ownership exempts the vet from any individual drug records
ELDU records (condition treated, species, dosage, duration, number of animals) must be kept at least 2 years and made available to the FDA on request
Any volunteer may initiate the extra-label regimen without veterinary authorization
An NPI number must first be obtained from the DEA before dispensing
e: AMDUCA requires a valid VCPR, 2-year ELDU record-keeping (species, condition, dosage, duration, animal counts) available to the FDA, and proper labeling. Laypersons cannot initiate ELDU.

q: A technician asks to give the full daily dose of an oral beta-lactam as one large q24h bolus to save handling. You should:
o: Approve — beta-lactams are concentration-dependent and best when peak is 8–10× MIC
Approve — penicillin frequency does not affect efficacy as long as AUC/MIC is 30–100
Deny — beta-lactams are time-dependent (Time > MIC); efficacy needs unbound drug above MIC for ~half the dosing interval, so consolidating doses causes failure
Deny — beta-lactams use oxygen-dependent transport active only in early morning
e: Beta-lactams are time-dependent: keep unbound concentration above MIC for ≥40–50% of the interval. A single large bolus lets levels fall below MIC and fails. Concentration-dependent (high peak) killing is the aminoglycoside pattern.

q: A director wants to replace an FDA-approved ophthalmic ointment with a paste mixed by a volunteer from bulk raw drug powders bought online. The primary hazard is:
o: Bulk-compounded products skip standard manufacturing requirements, risking improper potency/safety that prolongs suffering, lengthens treatment and raises total costs
Bulk compounding is legal for food animals but banned for cats
Mixing bulk drugs converts acquired resistance into innate structural resistance
The FDA requires bulk-compounded drugs to be exact copies of commercial products
e: Compounding from bulk raw ingredients bypasses FDA manufacturing/potency standards. Poor potency causes treatment failure and more suffering, ultimately driving costs up — the opposite of the intended saving.

q: An isolate's MIC is well below the fluoroquinolone breakpoint, yet dogs with hemorrhagic pneumonia fail to improve on correct dosing. The most logical explanation is:
o: Susceptibility testing has 0% true correlation with in vivo response
Fluoroquinolones lose all activity if given more often than every 48 h
The drug fails to penetrate the consolidated lung tissue, or is inactivated within the purulent microenvironment of the lesions
Innate resistance from an unmapped lack of cell walls
e: Susceptible-in-vitro can still fail in vivo: anatomical barriers (poor penetration of consolidated lung/sanctuary sites) and microenvironmental inactivation (purulent debris, low-O2/acidic foci) are the classic reasons.
